title: Data Sufficiency
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Data Sufficiency. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Avoid hidden assumptions and outside information

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
What sufficiency asks

Data-sufficiency questions ask whether the supplied statements determine a unique answer to the target question. You do not need to calculate the answer when a clear uniqueness test is enough.

Test statements systematically

Evaluate statement I alone, then statement II alone, then both together if neither is sufficient. A statement is sufficient only if it produces one answer under all stated conditions. Try distinct valid values to prove insufficiency.

Information discipline

Use only facts stated or standard definitions. Do not assume a variable is positive, an integer, or a particular shape unless the question says so. Check edge cases, zero denominators and ambiguous interpretations.

Worked example: Asked for integer (\(x\)), statement I says (\(x+y=10\)), and statement II says (\(y=4\)). I alone leaves many pairs; II alone gives no x. Together, (\(x=6\)), a unique value, so both are required.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Keep the target question visible while testing the statements.
  • Use counterexamples to show a statement is insufficient.
  • Check whether the requested result is a value, a yes/no decision, or a comparison.
  • Do not solve more than the question requires.
  • When both statements are combined, confirm there is still only one admissible answer.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Sufficient means enough to determine exactly one answer, not merely to produce an equation.
  • For a yes/no target, all valid cases must lead to the same yes or no.
  • For a numerical target, two different possible values prove insufficiency.
  • Do not import assumptions absent from the question.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    What is (\(x\))? I. (\(x+y=10\)). II. (\(x-y=2\)).

    1. Statement I alone
    2. Statement II alone
    3. Both together; neither alone
    4. Each alone
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Both together; neither alone

    Each statement alone allows multiple pairs. Together, adding the equations gives (\(2x=12\)), so (\(x=6\)) uniquely. The two statements together are sufficient.

  2. Core:

    Is (\(x>0\))? I. (\(x^2=9\)). II. (\(x\ne-3\)).

    1. Statement I alone
    2. Statement II alone
    3. Both together; neither alone
    4. Each alone
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Both together; neither alone

    Statement I alone gives (\(x=3\)) or (\(-3\)), so it is insufficient. Statement II alone permits positive and negative values, also insufficient. Together they force (\(x=3\)), so both statements together are sufficient.

  3. Foundation:

    What is the value of x? I: (\(x+y=9\)). II: (\(y=4\)).

    1. I alone is sufficient
    2. II alone is sufficient
    3. Both together are sufficient, neither alone is
    4. Each alone is sufficient
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Both together are sufficient, neither alone is

    I alone permits many pairs and II alone says nothing about x. Together, (\(x=9-4=5\)), uniquely.

  4. Standard:

    Is integer n even? I: (\(n^2\)) is even. II: (\(n\)) is divisible by 2.

    1. I alone is sufficient, II alone is not
    2. II alone is sufficient, I alone is not
    3. Both are individually sufficient
    4. Neither is sufficient
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: Both are individually sufficient

    An integer has an even square exactly when it is even, so statement I answers yes. Statement II directly says n is even. Each statement alone is sufficient.

  5. Challenge:

    Is (\(x>0\))? I: (\(x^2=9\)). II: (\(x^3>0\)).

    1. I alone is sufficient
    2. II alone is sufficient
    3. Both together are required
    4. Neither is sufficient
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: II alone is sufficient

    I permits x=3 or x=-3, so it is insufficient. II implies x>0, so II alone is sufficient.
